Since when are spies seen as credible sources?

I see the Leipzig story on a par with the recent Flydubai incident and the famous passport of a 9/11 attacker that was found undamaged at the WTC.

All three cases have one thing in common:

They provide, very early, very clearly, and very usefully exactly the blame and hero/victim narrative that benefits the respective political actors the most at that moment. At the same time, the operational incentives of the alleged perpetrator side (especially in Leipzig) are rather weak.

That doesn’t mean all three have to be false flags. It means that the narrative fit in all three cases is unusually high - and that in intelligence operations and highly political acts of violence, one should fundamentally expect the factor of an "information war." Professional services (Mossad, GRU, CIA, etc.) optimize not only the operation itself but also its public readability.

A healthy skepticism is therefore useful from a motivation perspective (who profits / benefits).

But if Ukraine ever achieves a manpower advantage on the front, then the frontline will start rolling in the other direction. Which is politically also not acceptable for the Kremlin.

So Russia needs to change strategies. And the easiest move they still have left is to convince the Russian people that Russia is not fighting in Ukraine against Ukrainians, but that Russia is fighting in Russia against NATO. NATO does not want to give the Kremlin this excuse, as that excuse would enable the Kremlin to switch to 'normal' mobilization. Instead NATO is trying to make this mobilization politically impossible for the Kremlin.
